item.title: After Accolades Abroad, an Israeli Documentary Faces a Backlash at Home
item.description:
When “NAZA,” a documentary about the killing of Palestinian civilians by Israeli forces in Gaza, premiered at the Venice International Film Festival last week, the Israeli directors received a 25-minute standing ovation. The film also won the Special Jury Prize.

But in Israel, the film has whipped up a storm of official criticism, as well as pushback from the military, which rarely weighs in on matters of the silver screen. On Monday, the Israeli military chief, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, consulted with top generals about how to respond to the film, saying it is “based on blood libels” and “deliberate distortions of reality.” He said the military would examine possible legal measures against those suspected of disseminating false allegations and of disclosing classified materials.

Israel’s minister of culture, Miki Zohar, went so far as to ask the authorities to examine whether the directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, could be stripped of their Israeli citizenship on grounds of “betraying the state of Israel.”

Representatives for Mr. Abraham and Ms. Szor declined to respond specifically to Mr. Zohar’s accusation and threat. But Mr. Abraham responded to criticism from home in a video statement on Sunday, saying that it was important for Israeli society to learn about the military’s actions in Gaza and that the soldiers had spoken in Hebrew “because they want to reach the Israeli public.”

The 80-minute documentary, co-produced by The Guardian, consists of interviews with 24 people described as Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers who, according to the film’s synopsis, reveal in detail “the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.”

The interviewees, who could potentially face legal consequences in Israel and abroad, were not identified.

The Guardian issued a statement on Monday saying that it was “disturbed to see the authoritarian response to ‘NAZA’ in Israel” and that the film was based on more than three years of investigative journalism.

“We will robustly defend NAZA — and the team behind it — from any attacks or attempts at censorship,” the statement added.

Almost three years after the Hamas-led attack against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which ignited the devastating war in Gaza, the reaction in Israel crystallizes the stark contrast between the country’s self-image and how it is increasingly seen from the outside.

The supercharged atmosphere of a political campaign ahead of national elections in October has further fueled the backlash.

Israelis are deeply divided over how to apportion blame for the policy, military and intelligence failures that preceded the attack and the war. But Israelis still largely view themselves as the victims of Oct. 7. The militants’ attack killed about 1,200 people in Israel, and about 250 more were taken hostage, according to the Israeli authorities. It was the deadliest day in the country’s history.

Only a small minority of Israelis have protested against the military’s conduct in the war, with most viewing it as a just campaign of self-defense.

Conversely, many abroad view Israel’s counteroffensive as excessive. More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed, including thousands of children, according to the Gaza health ministry, whose data does not distinguish between combatants and civilians. Much of Gaza had been left in ruins, and human rights groups and foreign governments have accused Israel of war crimes.

The domestic furor over the film has erupted though it has not yet been distributed and few in Israel have seen it.

“NAZA” is a Hebrew acronym for nezek agavi, or collateral damage. In the film, it is used to refer to the loosening of targeting constraints that increased the number of uninvolved civilians who could be put at risk by Israeli military attacks in Gaza carried out on the basis of mass surveillance aided by artificial intelligence.

The New York Times reported in December 2024 that on the first day of the war, Israel’s military leadership changed its rules of engagement, granting mid-ranking Israeli officers the authority to strike thousands of military sites and militants, including low-ranking fighters, and risk killing up to 20 civilians in each strike.

The Times investigation found that Israel had severely weakened its system of safeguards meant to protect civilians and adopted flawed methods to find targets and assess the risk of civilian casualties.

In the documentary “NAZA,” one interviewee says that Israel knowingly launched strikes that had killed 20, 30 or even 300 civilians, and that in one case approval was given for a strike that could kill 500.

The Israeli military denied that specific accusation in a social media post, saying that it “never planned, approved or carried out a strike in Gaza in which 500 civilians or anything near that number were anticipated to be killed.” It said it had operated in accordance with international law.

The military, which has viewed only excerpts, excoriated the documentary for showing anonymous testimonies “from individuals whose identity cannot be verified.”

The military and commentators in the news media also faulted the documentary for failing to acknowledge what they said was the strategy of Hamas to embed its fighters and military infrastructure among civilians.

Israeli politicians who oppose the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also attacked the documentary.

Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist vying for the premiership and a former military chief who lost a son in the fighting in Gaza, said it presented a “distorted” picture and demonstrated “moral blindness” and “detachment from reality.”

“Criticism is legitimate in a democratic society, but there is an abyss between it and smearing the good name of our soldiers in order to reap applause at festivals abroad,” he wrote in a social media post.

Mr. Abraham, for his part, said in his video statement that he hoped the film would be distributed widely in Israel and suggested that those now attacking it should “watch it, first of all.”

item.title: Israeli Strikes in Gaza Kill Teenager and Civil Defense Worker, Local Official Says
item.description:
Israeli airstrikes in a residential Gaza neighborhood on Tuesday killed a teenager and a civil defense worker, according to a local official, amid mounting international pressure on Israel to halt its attacks in the enclave.

The Israeli military said that it had “directed an attack against Hamas terrorists” and that the outcome in the Gaza City attack was “under review.” The Israeli operation in Gaza followed strikes in the past day that the military said had killed Hamas militants.

On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood of Gaza City killed a teenager, identified as Mohammed al-Zinati, 15, and wounded other people, a member of the civil defense team, Motaz Ayyoub, said in a phone interview.

A second drone strike less than a minute later killed Sharif Labad, a civil defense worker who was not on duty but had rushed to the scene, Mr. Ayyoub said. He said that he and Mr. Labad had been planning to meet and attend a wedding when his friend responded to the earlier strike.

“We are now in the mosque to do the funeral prayer,” Mr. Ayyoub said.

In separate statements on Tuesday, the Israeli military said that it had killed a Hamas commander in the northern Gaza Strip overnight and that it had killed two Hamas operatives on Monday, one in the Khan Younis area in southern Gaza and another in Gaza City.

Late on Tuesday, the Israeli military also said it struck “a senior Hamas terrorist” in the southern Gaza Strip. The office of Israel’s prime minister and minister of defense said in a joint statement that the strike had targeted the commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade and vowed that “Hamas will not remain in Gaza.”

Israel has continued to carry out deadly strikes in Gaza over the past six weeks, despite efforts by President Trump’s Board of Peace to halt the attacks following its announcement in late July that Hamas had agreed to surrender its weapons. Under the disarmament framework, Israel was expected to halt its military operations in Gaza except in cases of immediate self-defense, but Israeli officials rejected the agreement.

A senior Board of Peace official recently criticized Israel’s continuing strikes during a speech at the United Nations, saying that they did not serve Israeli interests and only delayed the demilitarization of Gaza.

The Israeli military operations in Gaza are taking place as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is campaigning for re-election and portraying himself as key to the country’s security. Jared Kushner, the Trump envoy and son-in-law who has been working with the Board of Peace on plans for Gaza, said earlier this month that Mr. Netanyahu’s government was acting “a little irrational” ahead of the election.

Volker Turk, the United Nations human rights chief, called on Tuesday for international investigators to be allowed into all parts of Gaza to recover the remains of Palestinians still buried under rubble, and to help gather evidence of potential war crimes.

He said in a statement on social media that remains believed to be from 96 people from three Palestinian families were recovered this month, including many women and children. Noting that Palestinian officials have estimated that thousands of people may still be buried under rubble, he said the findings so far “may only be the tip of the iceberg” because “much of Gaza has been flattened by Israeli bombing or demolition and clearing by heavy machinery and explosives.”

Doctors Without Borders said on Sunday said that one of its humanitarian vehicles was damaged and an aid worker injured when an Israeli strike in Gaza City targeted a vehicle less than seven feet away from them. The group said in a post on social media that the aid vehicle was clearly identified and accused Israeli forces of showing “a blatant disregard for the safety of humanitarian and medical personnel.”

“Nowhere is safe in Gaza,” Doctors Without Borders said, calling for civilians, health care workers and other humanitarian staff to be protected.

The Israeli military said in a statement that the attack in Gaza City on Sunday had targeted and killed two Hamas military wing operatives. The Israeli military said that it took steps to mitigate harm to civilians, including using “precise munitions and aerial surveillance.”

The Israeli military’s prosecution of the war in Gaza has come under further scrutiny in the past week after “NAZA,” a documentary about Palestinian civilian deaths in the war, premiered at the Venice International Film Festival. The Israeli directors received a 25-minute standing ovation and won the Special Jury Prize, but faced an official backlash at home.

The Israeli military chief, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, consulted on Monday with top generals about how to respond to the film, saying it was based on “deliberate distortions of reality.”

On Tuesday, at a ceremony marking the start of the Jewish New Year, Maj. Gen. Yaniv Asor, who leads the military’s southern command, insisted on the importance of “maintaining the integrity of our own conduct, distinguishing between the enemy and those who are not involved in the hostilities.” He said this required the military to examine itself and “correct what must be corrected.”

But General Asor also said that Israeli forces would continue to operate in Gaza “to prevent Hamas from rebuilding its capabilities.”

item.title: Does the Stork’s Return to Britain Restore History or Rewrite It?
item.description:
The noisy throng of birds beat their wings and hopped up and down in their pen. These 3-month-old white storks, fueled by a generous morning’s feed, were ready for takeoff.

As a keeper twisted open the gate of the pen, a dedicated crowd of bird watchers in stork-themed shirts held its collective breath from several hundred feet away. The sight of a juvenile stork on its first flight is not to be missed.

The lanky bird, fabled in European folklore as a bringer of life, is now a permanent addition to Britain’s skies. It is also a surprisingly contentious one.

To the conservationists behind the yearslong effort to establish a population, the storks’ introduction restores a species that was presumed to have been wiped out in Britain some 600 years ago. To some more skeptical naturalists, it is a misguided act that introduces a bird that had never made Britain its home.

The White Stork Project, as the effort is known, has so far established a colony of some 100 birds at Knepp, a 3,500-acre former dairy farm in West Sussex.

Over two decades, the environment has done most of the reclamation there unaided as part of a wider “rewilding” effort that lets natural processes govern the landscape. But Isabella Tree, the conservationist who co-owns Knepp, is giving it something of a push with the storks.

Unlike other birds that could strike out and breed from just one pair, storks are a sociable species that are more likely to survive in a colony, she said.

To build that colony, conservationists have released captive-bred storks at Knepp every summer for the past eight years. The effort is working: Some 40 nests silhouette the landscape’s oak canopies.

This year’s batch of fledglings was bred at a zoo from flightless birds that had crashed into electrical pylons in Poland. After mingling with the colony’s existing population of wild-hatched chicks, the juveniles are embarking on a thousand-mile seasonal migration to northern Africa this fall. It is a grueling voyage: Most typically die in the attempt, but survivors will return three or four years later to find a mate.

Ms. Tree’s hope is that the colony will eventually become self-sufficient and spread across southern England to form satellite colonies. “We know that we can bring them back,” she said in an interview in July.

As the colony has grown, so has a re-examination of the archaeological and written record of its existence.

Though white storks have been spotted in Britain over the centuries, some researchers say there is little sign they made more than fleeting visits.

“We have no evidence from any source whatsoever that there were ever areas in Britain with a significant stork population,” said Ulrich Schmölcke, an archaeologist who specializes in birds at the Leibniz Center for Archaeology in Mainz, Germany.

By that logic, Knepp might be Britain’s first white stork colony ever.

The question has opened a ferocious debate over how actively conservationists should reshape the wilderness.

Archaeologists have unearthed the occasional adult white stork bone in Britain, but they have never found juvenile remains that would show the birds were not just visitors, Dr. Schmölcke said.

Nor do white storks appear in Britain’s rich canon of folk tales or written laws, he pointed out, as they do in parts of Europe where they are unquestionably native breeders.

The evidence, Dr. Schmölcke said, suggested “they never established a stable population.”

Ian Carter, an ornithologist who previously worked with the official environmental body Natural England, objected to the managed release of white storks on that basis. “No matter how many times people say it’s a ‘reintroduction,’ it absolutely isn’t,” he said.

The birds could pose a threat to existing wildlife, because they breed in high densities and prey on vulnerable wetland creatures, Mr. Carter said. “You can’t impose a species on the environment without having knock-on effects on other species,” he added. “And it changes the meaning of wildlife if you can just pick and choose any bird.”

The uproar prompted Natural England to weigh in with an assessment. In May, it said it had determined that white storks were never a native breeding bird.

Although the birds had visited from continental Europe, researchers could locate only a single historical reference to a nesting pair: In 1416, a Scottish priest observed two white storks building a nest on the roof of St Giles’ Cathedral in Edinburgh before they flew off. It was not clear from the text whether they bred successfully.

“It’s an animal that has turned up here sporadically,” said Tony Juniper, the chairman of Natural England. “But we can’t convince ourselves yet that this was an established species.”

While Mr. Juniper was effusive about the broader effort to “rewild” Knepp with native plants and other animals, he said the environmental authorities could not actively support the introduction of a species without an established breeding history in Britain.

In response to the skeptics, Ms. Tree said the standard of evidence they demanded — juvenile remains or legal records mentioning breeding — was impossibly high.

Storks were part of medieval Britain, she said, pointing to their appearance in artworks and place names. One is Storrington, a village near Knepp.

“Ultimately, you can argue either way,” Ms. Tree said. “And I don’t think it matters.”

The birds’ prominence as a symbol of fertility persists in cartoons and old-fashioned euphemisms about childbirth. A common theory for the link traces it to migration patterns: Storks would return to the skies of medieval Europe in February and March, coinciding with increases in human births around nine months after midsummer weddings.

Germanic mythology held that storks delivered the souls of newborn babies from subterranean lakes, said Ms. Tree, who is writing a book on the birds. In the early 19th century, the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen adapted that idea in “The Storks,” a short story with a depiction of long-legged birds delivering newborns.

Bringing the birds to England has justifications beyond historical rectitude, Ms. Tree said. The storks’ large nests provide homes and food for other birds, she said. And the storks benefit from access to a cooler climate as continental Europe warms.

“We need to allow species to be able to move north in response to climate change,” she said.

While Ms. Tree’s critics contest her rationale, their objections are not a serious obstacle to her work. The releases at Knepp are independently funded and do not require official permission.

Mr. Juniper and Dr. Schmölcke both said that storks from mainland Europe could push north into Britain as the climate changes, regardless of the effort at Knepp.

At the estate in July, debates over their presence did not seem to concern the young storks as they took flight. Humans may have started the colony, but the birds did what feathered creatures tend to do. One by one they emerged from the pen, outstretched their wings and, after a few false starts, took flight.

Days later, the birds had embarked on their migration across the English Channel. Within weeks, some had been spotted in Morocco, scavenging in a garbage dump.

Jamie Craig, the zookeeper who had opened the pen to free the birds, responded with a resigned laugh to the image of them feasting on trash. “That’s life, that’s nature,” he said. “If we give it a resource, it will use it.”

item.title: The World Economy Is Becoming Wary of the U.S.
item.description:
Global investors are balking at U.S. bonds. Talk of the dollar’s dwindling power is getting louder. Foreign governments are hauling their gold out of American vaults.

Almost two years into President Trump’s second term, the world economy is increasingly looking for ways to distance itself from America. Concerns about a $40 trillion debt burden, the excessive use of sanctions to solve foreign policy problems and Mr. Trump’s penchant for pushing the limits of the rule of law are raising questions about the appeal of the United States as a haven for global investment.

Despite pledges by foreign companies and nations to invest in the United States — in many cases to curry favor with the White House — capital is starting to seek alternative destinations.

“Geopolitical factors and U.S. weaponization of the dollar through financial sanctions are causing central banks and other official investors to attempt to diversify away from dollar assets,” said Eswar Prasad, the former head of the International Monetary Fund’s China division.

The United States is not yet an investment pariah. Private investors are still pouring money into American financial markets and stocks, artificial intelligence infrastructure is booming and no rival currency is poised to topple the dollar imminently.

In testimony before Congress on Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that he remained confident in the credibility of the U.S. financial system, arguing that bond auctions continue to operate successfully and that the dollar is still thriving as measured by its share of global transactions.

“The U.S. is in fact the leader, and the leader does not fear competition,” Mr. Bessent said. “Competition makes us better.”

But cracks in America’s economic dominance are starting to show.

The most glaring example has been in the bond market. Yields have been soaring as investors nervous about the mounting national debt demand a higher rate of return for buying Treasury bonds. This week, the yield on the 10-year Treasury topped 5 percent, reaching its highest level since 2007.

A decision to raise rates on Wednesday could help to alleviate concerns about the Fed’s grip on elevated inflation, fears that have injected more jitters into bond markets.

The ominous bond threshold was crossed a week after the Treasury Department purchased $5.2 billion of its own debt maturing in the next 10 to 20 years, part of a plan to inject demand into the Treasury market to try to push prices higher and yields lower. Mr. Bessent said investors were failing to understand the underlying strength of the economy and dared them to bet against him.

“It’s my dream,” Mr. Bessent said last week at Southern Methodist University. “I have asymmetric information. I am the house now.”

With the United States’ long-term fiscal situation looking shaky, some countries are starting to wonder if America is a wise investment. This month, Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, the largest in the world, said it planned to reduce its holdings of U.S. Treasuries as it looks elsewhere for stronger returns.

And then there is the future of the dollar.

Nearly 90 percent of global foreign exchange transactions are in dollars. But the share of dollars being held in central bank reserves has been steadily declining over the past decade, falling to 56 percent at the end of 2025 from 64 percent in 2015.

Last year, Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, said erratic policymaking in the United States was setting the stage for a “global euro moment.”

The United States has taken advantage of the greenback’s special status to use it as a foreign policy tool, imposing stiff sanctions on adversaries such as Iran and Russia. As the United States ramps up its use of sanctions to resolve global conflicts, the permanence of the dollar as the world’s reserve currency has come into question with greater frequency.

This year, the United States tried to start scaling back its sanctions program amid worries that an overuse of financial warfare was leading other countries to seek alternatives to the dollar. The dollar is used in most cross-border financial transactions, so sanctions can essentially cut off a country’s ability to interact with the Western financial system. Frustrated with how the United States uses its economic might, more countries are seeking alternative financial systems that America cannot touch.

However, Mr. Bessent reversed course in August when he announced Operation Economic Outcast. The initiative aims to strangle Iran’s economy and threatens secondary sanctions on any country that maintains economic ties to Tehran. Even the Treasury secretary acknowledged that if the United States is forced to make good on that threat, it could “blow up the global financial system.”

Although the euro and China’s renminbi do not appear ready to overtake the dollar anytime soon, the emergence of central bank digital currencies, stablecoins and cryptocurrencies give U.S. adversaries new avenues to circumvent the American financial system when making international transactions.

China has been leading the development of a cross-border digital currency platform with Hong Kong, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia that would allow money to move more quickly and with lower fees than what is possible with traditional banking transactions. A similar cross-border payments project led by some Group of 7 nations and Western financial institutions is also in development but is not as far along as China’s initiative, which is known as mBridge.

Russia and India said last week that they are working on a plan that would let them use central bank digital currencies to settle international trade payments. Such a mechanism would allow the countries to expand their trade relationship and reduce reliance on Western financial institutions that can be targeted by U.S. sanctions.

“The story of moving away from the dollar is one of the oldest stories that exists,” said Josh Lipsky, the chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council. “Countries have thought about working around the dollar, and technology is making it a little cheaper and easier to do it than before.”

While some countries are focused on digital money, others are going for the gold as they fret about the stability of the United States.

In 2025, world international reserves held in gold surpassed foreign official holdings of U.S. Treasury securities. This year, the price of gold exceeded $5,000 per troy ounce for the first time in history as central banks stocked up on the metal amid intensifying global conflicts and concerns over inflation.

Demand for gold is so high that some countries also want to keep theirs closer to home. With geopolitical unrest rising and Mr. Trump lobbing tariff threats against European allies, some have even taken the rare step of relocating the gold that they keep in vaults at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

This month, the central bank of the Netherlands said it transferred a large part of its 95 tons of North American gold reserves out of the United States, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest” and the need to be prepared for crisis. In March, the Bank of France said it pulled 129 tons of gold from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and moved it to Paris.

The Trump administration has not threatened to seize foreign gold held in the United States, but Mr. Trump has raised questions about his views of international law by floating the idea of colonizing places like Greenland and Canada.

“It’s like the countries don’t trust the U.S.,” said Daniel Tannebaum, who served as the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control compliance coordinator for the New York Fed. “I do think that there is a fear factor.”

That fear factor is also creating blowback for American companies that are trying to do business abroad.

Mr. Tannebaum, who is a partner in Oliver Wyman’s risk and public policy practice, said that the aggressive use of tariffs and export controls by the United States has made European countries and companies wary of adopting American technology for sensitive industries such as artificial intelligence. They worry that if they are dependent on the United States for such infrastructure it could be used against them if Washington decides to ban or disable the technology, as it has done during disputes with China and Russia.

All of this has contributed to an erosion of America’s status as a safe haven.

“Governments and companies now have to ask what would happen if the United States turned its economic leverage against them,” Mr. Tannebaum said.

item.title: In the Maldives, A.I. Is Helping to Rebuild Beaches Lost to Rising Seas
item.description:
As the world’s oceans grow ever warmer and the seas rise ever higher, coastlines are retreating at a record pace. And with the rising tides, thousands of coastal communities are at risk. The United Nations warns that as many as 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050.

But in the Maldives, a low-lying archipelago in the Indian Ocean, researchers are doing something remarkable: They’re growing beaches.

The project, born in a lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology a decade ago, uses artificial intelligence, satellite and ocean current data to predict coastal erosion patterns and create submerged structures that harness currents to coax the beach back.

The company, Coastal Assembly, has regrown the sandy shore, extending the beach some 90 feet toward the ocean. A second project built a new sandbar with more than 30,000 cubic feet of sand in just six months, stirring hope that there may be a way to slow the disappearance of coastal societies.

In the turquoise waters off Kaafu Atoll, the company’s automated intelligence analyzed 10 years of satellite imagery, currents and other data to predict erosion patterns. Then the company designed and installed 54 structures cast from marine concrete blended with sand and crushed shells, arranged in a row of hexagons. The structure is specially designed to break up eroding waves while allowing the flow of currents that accumulate sand and sediment.

Early results are promising. But perhaps most consequential is the technology that predicts and monitors coastal losses. Researchers say it has the potential to aid communities in adapting to climate change by reducing the time and cost of complex coastline modeling, and predicting the areas most vulnerable to erosion.

According to a May report from the United Nations, a lack of data and satellite observations has hindered climate adaptation among island nations. Increased data mapping, a U.N. report in 2026 said, is a “critical foundation” for effective adaptation to climate change.

But the recent boom in satellites and earth-observation technologies, combined with the rapid development of artificial intelligence has made low-cost, automated monitoring and prediction possible, said Skylar Tibbits, one of Coastal Assembly’s founders.

“It took us months to do one site in the beginning,” Mr. Tibbits said. Site surveying, experimentation, computational simulations and calculations, “everything was by hand.” Now, the small team can predict future erosion and develop a plan to address it within a day. They’re monitoring erosion patterns in real time at nearly 1,000 coastal sites using the technology, he said.

“We can go to any community around the world and understand what has happened and then propose a solution that is very precisely tailored to them,” Mr. Tibbits said.

So far, the trials have shown promising results. Not only has the beach roughly doubled in size, but new coral has grown on the underwater structures, and fish and other marine wildlife have come to inhabit them, said Srikanth Devarapalli, general manager of the resort that hosts the pilot.

Coastal Assembly spun off from M.I.T. late last year as a public benefit company and had previously received funding from the United States Agency for International Development and National Geographic before raising several million dollars in venture-backed investment. Now, the company has 10 more installations set for the Maldives and more projects planned in the Bahamas, Boston Harbor and Miami.

Of course, the dynamics of coastal erosion are complex. Sand and sediment are always eroding and accumulating with seasonal currents, and sea levels are continuing to rise as the world warms. It remains to be seen just how effective the new beach will be in protecting the coast in the long run, how long the beaches might last, or how widely the concept could spread. But the early results have garnered support.

“I have seen it,” said Mohamed Nasheed, who served as President of the Maldives from 2008 to 2012. “It actually works.”

Perhaps nowhere is more vulnerable to climate change than his island nation. Storms are growing more frequent and intense, bringing surging surf. Increasingly strong marine heat waves are killing the coral reefs that protect coastlines, Mr. Nasheed said, and man-made harbors have further accelerated erosion.

“All of this adds up to a major challenge for the islands,” he said. “You have schools falling, you have roads being washed away, houses being washed way.”

Traditional sea walls, water breaks or other “huge concrete solutions” are prohibitively expensive and won’t solve the problem, he said, and neither will sand pumping or dredging, which can damage coastal ecosystems and requires repeated investment as sand washes away. Solutions that work with nature, rather than against it, Mr. Nasheed said, must be adopted quickly “to meet the ferocity of the waves coming to us.”

The technology developed by Coastal Assembly offers a “very, very concrete solution,” said Hyun Kim, Senior Advisor at the Global Centre for Climate Mobility, which is hosted through the United Nations. “They’re able to reverse the effect of sea level rise.” Mr. Kim said the organization was working to facilitate and fund the technology in other low-lying states and the millions of communities facing coastal erosion.

item.title: The Canaduropean Union?
item.description:
President Trump has called Canada the 51st state, but will the country become instead the 28th state — of the European Union? The E.U.’s offer of an associate membership to Canada has prompted excitement and confusion in equal measure.

In January, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada declared a “rupture in the world order” and called for middle powers to band together. I wondered at the time what he meant, and this might be part of it. But what would bringing Canada into the E.U. mean? What would it mean for Europe, whose geography as much as its values have always defined its borders, at least so far? And for Canada, whose own geography is the reason it’s been so dependent on the United States?

Today my colleagues Matina Stevis-Gridneff, who’s on the road with Carney, and Jeanna Smialek, who covers the E.U., write about the trickiness of inventing a new world order.

By Matina Stevis-Gridneff and Jeanna Smialek

To many observers, a tighter alliance between the European Union and Canada seems to make sense.

Trump has waged a relentless trade war with Canada, challenging its economy. The U.S. has also pulled back support for NATO and Ukraine, leaving the E.U. scrambling to shore up its defenses. That vacuum has left both Canada and the E.U. looking for new partners as the alliances established after World War II shift.

The invitation for Canada to become an “associate member” of the E.U., made yesterday by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, shows just how intent these two traditional U.S. allies are on pursuing a stabler future by binding closer together. “We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in a speech, as Carney sat next to her, beaming.

Between them, the E.U.’s 27 members and Canada have more than 490 million citizens, four of the world’s 10 largest economies, and a whole lot of desire to find partners outside the U.S. Carney often calls Canada “the most European non-European country.” E.U. leaders have spent years joking that it could join the bloc if only it were not on a far-flung landmass.

But yesterday’s announcement — which still falls well short of full membership — also highlighted the challenges involved in remaking the world order in real time. It may be easier said than done.

The 28th state?

The E.U. hinges on deep, dense legal and procedural rules, built over decades by a group of nations that ceded sovereignty to one another, and to an unelected executive branch in Brussels.

Bringing in a country an ocean away is not straightforward.

Canada does not actually qualify for full E.U. membership, since, ultimately, it’s not in Europe. But bringing it closer to the E.U. is still complicated. And the initiative began raising eyebrows within minutes of being announced on the floor of the European Parliament.

The issue was the name. The label the European Union wants to confer on Canada, “associate member,” is not an existing type of partnership. It has no obvious legal basis, and it’s not entirely clear what it would even entail.

The term has drawn consternation from several member states, who see it as vague, untethered from legal frameworks and potentially unfair to countries that already have detailed legal agreements with the E.U. That includes candidate nations such as Albania and also Britain and Norway, who have deep trade and defense ties to the bloc.

Some in Canada don’t appear to love it either. The Conservative opposition leader seized on the term, arguing that if Canada was to never be the 51st state of the U.S., it should also not become the 28th member state of the E.U.

Hours after von der Leyen spoke, the incoming Canadian ambassador to the E.U. said that Canada preferred “alliance for the future” to describe the emerging new bond with the E.U. “I think we’re still a ways away from actually landing on what we think the best way to describe it is,” he said.

Middle powers, acting together?

Ultimately, most experts agree the point is the symbolism.

item.title: Why Israel Wants More One-Ton Bombs From the U.S. and Why the Sale Is Controversial
item.description:
The Trump administration’s decision to send 60,000 powerful one-ton bombs to Israel as part of a $2.8 billion deal — one of the largest arms agreements ever — will allow Israel to replenish its supply of a munition it considers vital.

The weapons became the focus of great tension between the Biden administration and Israel after one-ton bombs were widely used in densely populated areas of Gaza where Israel had steered civilians for their safety.

With opposition to military assistance to Israel growing in Washington, such a huge sale of heavy bombs, paid for by the U.S. government, could be an effort by the administration to stock up the Israeli arsenal before political shifts in the United States make such shipments impossible, analysts said. It is certain to set off an outcry in Congress.

The Israeli military pivoted toward the use of the one-ton bombs after the Hamas-led attack against southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, drastically changing its shopping list, U.S. government data show. In 2025, Israel bought nearly eight times as many one-ton bombs from the United States as it did from 2012 to 2015.

Israel’s emphasis on buying and using some of the largest bombs currently made runs counter to that of most other modern militaries, which have been making their aerial munitions smaller and even more accurate in the hopes of limiting civilian casualties during combat.

Israel has used a vast amount of the one-ton bombs in large part to target the tunnel network Hamas developed in Gaza for its fighters, weapons and command centers. Israeli officials have said that Hamas fighters intentionally embed themselves among civilians, forcing the Israeli military to risk killing civilians.

A New York Times investigation in December 2023 found that the Israeli military routinely used one-ton bombs in the weeks immediately after the 2023 attack and identified more than 200 instances of Israel dropping the powerful munitions, including in densely populated areas.

Here is a closer look at the transaction and its significance.

According to a U.S. official, Israel will receive 20,000 Mk-84 bombs and another 20,000 BLU-117 bombs. The two types of one-ton bombs are nearly identical.

The bombs are highly versatile, experts say. They can be set to detonate above ground, sending shrapnel 1,000 feet in any direction, or, with delayed fuses, set to explode underground. They can be fitted with kits that allow them to hit targets with precision and from a long range. The craters from one-ton bombs can be up to 50 feet deep.

In addition to the 40,000 Mk-84 and BLU-117 bombs, Israel will also receive 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads, which explode on delay after busting through a surface like soil, rock or concrete, the U.S. official said. They also weigh a ton each, but because their casings are thicker and far heavier, they carry far less explosive power than the Mk-84 and BLU-117 bombs.

According to the U.S. Army office that oversees bomb procurement, “ideal targets” for one-ton bombs “are buildings, rail yards and lines of communication.” The 250- and 500-pound bombs more typically used by the U.S. military are designed for “soft, fragment sensitive targets” like troops, fuel storage tanks and radars, the office said.

The $2.8 billion purchase is being funded from the Pentagon’s budget for foreign military sales. That means the money effectively flows from U.S. taxpayers to Israel’s military and then to U.S. munitions manufacturers.

While congressional leaders can tell the administration they oppose the transaction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio can exercise emergency powers to proceed with it.

Mr. Rubio has repeatedly done just that, including in March, when he bypassed Congress to send $4 billion in weaponry to Israel, including more than 35,000 of the same kinds of one-ton bombs.

Opposition is likely to be heated. Some Democrats in Congress have called for ending U.S. military aid, or even all aid, to Israel in response to the huge civilian toll of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the Oct. 7 attacks on Israel.

Anger toward Israel is also growing on the right. The former Fox News host Tucker Carlson, an outspoken critic of Israel, wrote in a social media post on Tuesday that there was no justification for supplying Israel with so many of the bombs it had used in killing Palestinians in Gaza. He said it would only embolden Israel elsewhere.

“The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region,” he wrote. “If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do.”

Experts describe one-ton bombs as a workhorse of the Israeli Air Force, which has operated in seven theaters of conflict over the past few years: Gaza, the occupied West Bank, Lebanon, Iran, Syria, Yemen and Iraq.

Those campaigns have severely depleted the air force’s munitions. One former air force commander, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive information, said that Israel had learned it was necessary to amass a multiyear supply, in case of delays in replenishing stocks, and that 40,000 one-ton bombs were considered a full supply.

“The traditional concept of Israel’s defense doctrine was short wars,” said a retired major general, Amos Yadlin, a former deputy air force commander and former head of Israeli military intelligence. “What we saw in the last three years was Israel was dragged — and maybe even with some contributions of Israeli decisions — to a long war. And if you’re in a strategy of long wars, you need more ammunition.”

The New York Times reported in December 2023 that in the first six weeks of the war in Gaza, Israel routinely used one-ton bombs in parts of the enclave that it had designated as safe for civilians, including densely populated areas. The Times identified 208 craters of at least 40 feet across in an area of southern Gaza where Israel had ordered civilians to move to for their own safety.

Munitions experts say that bombs of that size are almost never dropped by U.S. forces in densely populated areas, and U.S. military officers have said such bombs are unsuitable for urban combat. Since the Vietnam War, U.S. forces have used one-ton bombs sparingly.

Israel reaches for them far more often. It says that the heavy bombs are necessary to strike enemy forces hiding in large buildings or in underground tunnels, and that its military always seeks to avoid or minimize civilian casualties.

The one-ton bombs became a source of friction between President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in May 2024, when Mr. Biden held up a shipment of 1,800 bombs in an effort to deter Israel from attacking the city of Rafah, where many displaced Palestinians were sheltering.

Israel attacked and destroyed much of Rafah anyway. The Trump White House released the shipment of bombs days after Donald J. Trump took office in 2025.

At a time when the relationship between Mr. Trump and Mr. Netanyahu has been on a roller-coaster ride, the political dimensions of proceeding with such a large deal for heavy bombs cannot be ignored.

Chuck Freilich, a former Israeli deputy national security adviser, said the deal should not be seen as an attempt to aid Mr. Netanyahu’s campaign for a new term in next month’s election, in which he is behind in the polls. “If it was a new deal for F-35s, it would be worth a headline,” he said.

Still, General Yadlin said, the arms deal sends an important signal to Israel’s enemies that the United States still has its back. “This is a way to show that, even if there are some differences, on the basic security of Israel, the U.S. is still a very strong ally,” he said.

But Israel’s defenders are also mindful that the political winds have shifted and that it is not likely to become any easier to obtain such munitions from the United States in the foreseeable future, especially ahead of the 2028 election.

Jesse Weinberg, a researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, said that officials in Israel and many of Israel’s supporters in Washington were looking to “front-load” military aid to Israel “because we don’t know what the construction of the next Congress is going to be — and then there’s the eye to 2028.”

“The view at the Kirya,” he said of Israel’s military headquarters, “in the prime minister’s office and also among Israel’s supporters on the Hill is that if you want to move things, now is the time.”

item.title: U.S. Intelligence Warns of China Theft Over Sale of F-35 Jets to Saudis
item.description:
U.S. intelligence officers have expressed concerns in internal reports about possible Chinese espionage related to a pending sale of dozens of advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia valued at $24 billion, according to American officials.

Intelligence analysts have raised the possibility that China could acquire F-35 jet technology through spying in Saudi Arabia or through its military and security partnership with the kingdom, the U.S. officials said.

One detailed report issued by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency months ago discusses Chinese military access to Saudi bases and Saudi Arabia’s use of Chinese technology in its telecommunications infrastructure, an official said. It also questions whether the Americans and Saudis will be able to maintain secure sites for the F-35 technology, the official said.

That report has circulated among several administration agencies and congressional offices, as have assessments from other intelligence offices. The D.I.A. issued a more general report in the fall of 2025 on similar risks when the administration was discussing the possibility of the sales, The New York Times reported at the time.

President Trump then announced the sale the day before he hosted Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia, at the White House in November.

The sale is at a more advanced stage now, and the newer D.I.A. report raises sharper concerns, including technical ones. The State Department sent the proposed sales package of 48 jets and a spare engine to two congressional committees in June to get informal approval. Some lawmakers and aides have been pressing the administration on the concerns raised by the intelligence agencies.

The U.S. officials spoke about the concerns among intelligence officials on the condition of anonymity because of sensitivities around espionage and military matters.

The State Department, the Pentagon and the Embassy of Saudi Arabia in Washington declined to comment. The White House and the embassy of China did not reply to requests for comment.

U.S. intelligence agencies raised similar concerns internally during Mr. Trump’s first term after he agreed in 2020 to sell F-35 jets to the United Arab Emirates as part of a deal in which the Emirates would normalize relations with Israel.

It takes years to produce the jets, which are made by Lockheed Martin, and the Biden administration decided to review the sale well before production and delivery. Intelligence agencies raised the same issues at that time because the Emirates was strengthening its military, intelligence and technology ties with China. U.S. officials then ended the sales process.

Prince Mohammed has been trying to build up his military. He began a disastrous seven-year war against the Houthis in Yemen, one in which Saudi-led forces killed civilians with American bombs. The Saudi military has failed to ward off attacks from Iran in the current U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, and the Saudis and the Houthis, which are supported by Iran, have begun fighting again.

Prince Mohammed has long sought to buy F-35 jets from the United States, and Mr. Trump finally agreed last November. Saudi Arabia and the United States have had decades of military cooperation, and the kingdom is by far the largest buyer of American weapons and defense equipment. But Saudi Arabia buys ballistic missiles from China, and the Chinese military is helping the Saudis learn to build ballistic missiles, set up production facilities and improve missile operations.

Democratic lawmakers sent President Joseph R. Biden Jr. a letter in June 2022 laying out their concerns over that program.

The recent Pentagon intelligence report said that only Saudi and American officers and contractors should have access to sites where F-35 technology would reside, a U.S. official said. Pentagon officials are especially concerned about protecting the advanced radar and surveillance technology of the F-35.

The intelligence analysts ask in the report whether Saudi Arabia would more broadly agree to limit contact with Chinese military and intelligence personnel and associated entities.

The report also questions whether Saudi officials would agree to remove equipment from Huawei and ZTE, two prominent Chinese technology companies, from telecommunications and router infrastructure and defense installations.

Some Israeli officials also have concerns about the deal, as they did when Mr. Trump proposed such sales to the Emirates. Israel is the only country in the Middle East that has F-35s, which it has deployed in airstrikes against Iran in recent years. Since the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, U.S. policymakers have tried to ensure that Israel maintains its “qualitative military edge” in the region, as mandated by Congress.

Previous administrations ran a highly classified, monthslong process to review whether proposed weapons sales in the region would meet that requirement. The second Trump administration has continued to push through large arms sales to Israel, however, despite calls across the American political spectrum to end or severely decrease military support.

In several instances, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has bypassed the congressional approval process to expedite shipments of weapons to Israel, citing an emergency in the region. If congressional leaders do not give approval for the F-35 jet sales, he could decide to do the same with that.

Mr. Trump has also agreed to help Saudi Arabia build a civilian nuclear program, a project that has raised its own security concerns because Prince Mohammed has vowed to build nuclear weapons if Iran does so.

item.title: Fiji Declares a National Emergency as H.I.V. Cases Skyrocket
item.description:
Fiji has declared a national crisis amid an extraordinary rise of H.I.V. cases, with health officials raising the alarm about an epidemic that has emerged alongside an increase in injectable drug use.

Fiji, a Pacific island nation of fewer than one million people, recorded more than 2,000 new H.I.V. cases in 2025 — 16 times as many as in 2019, the government said in an official statement on Tuesday. One in 60 adults on the archipelago is living with the virus that causes AIDS, the government estimated.

UNAIDS, a United Nations program, said in a statement on Wednesday that it was “one of the sharpest increases in new H.I.V. infections globally.”

Winnie Byanyima, the executive director of UNAIDS, added that Fiji’s epidemic was “a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over.”

The outbreak is not limited to particular areas or populations, health officials warned. And because the nation serves as a regional hub for business, tourism and transport, the surge in cases could affect other countries in the South Pacific if left unchecked.

That interconnectedness may have contributed to the soaring rates of infection, said Eamonn Murphy, the director of regional support teams in the Asia Pacific region, Central Asia and Eastern Europe for UNAIDS.

An influx of drugs on the islands during the coronavirus pandemic added “fuel on the flame” to a longstanding, but low-level, H.I.V. presence in Fiji, Mr. Murphy said.

The country is a key example in a growing trend of Pacific island nations “caught in the middle of illicit smuggling routes,” according to a 2024 U.N. report. As substances like methamphetamine and cocaine pass through Fiji and other island nations on their way to Australia and New Zealand, the report said, those nations have emerged as drug markets, not just way stations.

Fiji is also one of several global hot spots where a dangerous trend called “bluetoothing,” in which people inject themselves with the blood of other drug users to get a cheap high, is contributing to spikes in H.I.V. rates.

Health officials say they believe that drug use is a key driver of Fiji’s epidemic. A December report by the World Health Organization and United Nations Development Program found that nearly half of the H.I.V. patients with available information about their exposure had injected drugs, primarily crystal methamphetamine.

“Fiji was off the map in terms of H.I.V.,” Mr. Murphy said. But in recent years, the virus has spread throughout the country, heavily affecting young men but also raising mortality rates among children and babies born to infected women.

In its statement on Tuesday, the government said that 59 infants were born with H.I.V. in 2025, with 18 of them dying before their first birthday.

Fiji’s government has ramped up testing and treatment efforts since January 2025, when the nation declared an H.I.V. outbreak. But “an outbreak-level response is no longer sufficient,” Dr. Atonio Lalabalavu, the nation’s health minister, said in a video statement posted on Tuesday.

Fiji pledged a “whole-of-government response,” including expanded access to free testing, prevention services and treatment, as well as harm-reduction measures such as programs that allow people who inject drugs to exchange used needles for clean ones.

Mr. Murphy praised the government’s efforts, but said community leaders and the religious authorities would have to help combat the stigma around drug use and misunderstandings about H.I.V. and its treatments.

“They really need to move fast,” he said.

item.title: Warming Played ‘Very Strong’ Role in Himalayan Floods, Study Finds
item.description:
Industrial emissions have significantly warmed the snow-capped Himalayan region where a rock collapse caused devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet last month, researchers concluded in a report published Thursday in London. Rising temperatures very likely contributed to the disaster by destabilizing the ice and permafrost that underlay the mountain slopes, the report said.

The authors of the report, one of the first comprehensive scientific assessments of the catastrophe, acknowledged that climate change wasn’t the sole factor behind the floods.

A 2015 earthquake in Nepal might also have been a factor in priming the slope, near the country’s border with Tibet, to fall apart, the researchers said. The tumbling ice and debris combined with water and sediment in the valleys below last month to create a wall of mud that roared through towns, bridges and hydropower facilities.

Still, the new findings establish that human-caused warming had a “very strong linkage” to the disaster, said one of the report’s authors, Manjeet Dhakal, who leads the South Asia office of the research group Climate Analytics. Evidence of this connection could inform Nepal’s request for financial help from the United Nations’ fund for climate aid.

Three weeks after the disaster, the death toll stands at over 1,300. Thousands more people remain unaccounted for and are likely buried in the mud. Nepal estimates it will cost $5 billion to recover and rebuild.

The new assessment of the floods was prepared by two dozen researchers from around the globe and published by World Weather Attribution, a scientific initiative that evaluates the role of human-caused climate change in weather disasters. The report has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The researchers found that the days leading up the floods were much warmer than usual around the northern face of Langtang Lirung, the mountain where the rock and ice avalanche occurred. At the elevation where the rock detached, roughly 17,000 feet, the high temperatures that week were around 54 degrees Fahrenheit, or more than 12 degrees Fahrenheit above normal, the researchers found. July and August in the area were unusually warm overall, as global temperatures tied the record for Earth’s hottest month.

Global warming driven by burning fossil fuels has raised the mercury significantly around the high peaks of this part of the Himalayas compared with preindustrial levels, the scientists found. Over the decades, that has exposed the permafrost within the rocky slopes to above-freezing conditions more frequently.

In high mountains, permafrost — a mixture of soil and sediment held together by ice — acts as a sealant, keeping water from percolating into cracks in the bedrock. So when permafrost thaws, more water can seep in. Then, when the water refreezes, it pries the cracks open wider and weakens the rock, said Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands who contributed to the new report.

Higher temperatures have also shrunk the glacier on Langtang Lirung that had been helping to support part of the mountainside, Dr. Immerzeel said. The glacier’s retreat occurred gradually for nearly two centuries before accelerating in 2010, when it began to lose around 2 percent of its area per year, he said.

Something else that may have added to the deluge caused by the plunging ice and rock was the exceptionally large amount of snow that fell in the region last October and November, the researchers said. Extra rain or melted snow can also infiltrate into the bedrock and make it more prone to collapse. But the researchers didn’t find clear evidence that human-caused climate change was increasing summer or winter precipitation in the region.

item.title: State Department Extends Visa Ban on Abbas, Other Palestinian Officials
item.description:
The State Department announced Wednesday that it would continue to deny visas to Palestinian officials because of actions taken by their governing and political groups that “internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” including trying to bring cases to international tribunals.

The denial of visas would keep Mahmoud Abbas, the leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Palestinian Authority, from attending the annual United Nations General Assembly in New York. The main part of that conclave starts next week.

This marks the second year in a row that the Trump administration has prevented Mr. Abbas from attending. In August 2025, weeks before the United Nations meeting that year, the State Department said Secretary of State Marco Rubio had decided not to issue visas to Palestinian officials in order to hold them “accountable for not complying with their commitments, and for undermining the prospects for peace.”

The State Department demanded at the time that the two Palestinian groups “consistently repudiate terrorism,” including the Hamas-led attack in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and “end incitement to terrorism in education.” It also cited contacts between Palestinian officials and the International Criminal Court.

The Trump administration opposes Palestinians trying to bring cases to that court or the International Court of Justice.

About that time, the department also suspended issuing almost all types of visitor visas for anyone holding a Palestinian passport. That went well beyond earlier restrictions on visas of Palestinian visitors from Gaza.

The State Department said in a statement on Wednesday that it was extending the punitive visa measurements because the two Palestinian groups had not done enough to change their practices and were “glorifying terrorism.” The department said it had notified Congress of the visa ban extension.

item.title: A Corruption Case Spawns Memes and Indignation Among Ukrainians
item.description:
Ukrainians are used to revelations of corruption in their government. But one case that emerged this month has managed to grab their attention, in part because of a vivid turn of phrase.

An official working under Ukraine’s top prosecutor was caught on tape by anticorruption investigators describing his own approach to enriching himself through corruption.

“If you’re going to do something, then go all in — boom,” the official was recorded saying. He then explained, profanely, what he meant. If you’re going to sleep with a woman, he said, then sleep with “a queen.” And if you’re going to steal, then steal “a million.”

According to investigators, the official, Serhiy Kropyva, and others in the Office of the Prosecutor General did just that — the stealing part, anyway — through kickbacks they received for covering up a network of phone scammers working in Ukraine and abroad.

The allegations toppled the prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, who was formally removed from office on Tuesday by Parliament after President Volodymyr Zelensky called for his ouster. Mr. Kravchenko had already resigned last week.

He denies wrongdoing. He left Ukraine in recent days, saying that he was traveling abroad to discuss the work of anti-corruption bodies in Ukraine with partner countries — an explanation greeted with eye-rolls by his countrymen.

The official on the tape, Mr. Kropyva, has been arrested and is in pretrial detention. He at first denied that it was his voice but has since backed away from that claim. He says he is innocent of corruption.

The colorful recording has spawned memes as well as bitterness among Ukrainians. They have been sacrificing for their homeland, including through regular donations to the army, only to see an endless parade of officials accused of illicitly filling their own pockets.

Many Ukrainians see graft as a threat not only to the war effort but also to the country’s future. At the same time, they voice pride in the justice meted out in such cases, seeing it as a sign that the country’s democracy, including independent anti-corruption agencies, remains healthy after nearly five years of all-out war.

The scandal involving the Office of the Prosecutor General comes at a delicate moment for Mr. Zelensky, who has come under pressure to clean house amid the drip-drip-drip of corruption cases.

The revelations are especially stinging at a time when Ukraine is badly lacking money for the war. They threaten to sow doubts among the country’s European partners just as Ukraine asks for help in plugging its yawning budget gaps.

Russia has escalated attacks on the Ukrainian economy, striking warehouses, gas stations, railways and energy infrastructure with jet-powered drones for which Ukraine has not yet found an effective defense. The country’s prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, said last week that Russian assaults would deprive the state of about $1.5 billion.

A clash over Ukraine’s anti-corruption efforts came to a head last year, when people took to the streets to safeguard the autonomy of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, known as NABU, and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office. Both were created a decade ago with strong Western backing.

The Zelensky administration had moved to curb their power by placing them under the authority of the prosecutor general, who is approved by Parliament, where the president’s party holds a majority. Mr. Zelensky reversed course in the face of the demonstrations.

The prosecutor general who would have overseen the anti-corruption agencies was Mr. Kravchenko, the man who has now been felled in a corruption case.

Since the 2025 protests that preserved its independence, NABU has accused dozens of officials of corruption. The most highly publicized case, involving graft in the energy sector, led to the dismissal of Andriy Yermak, the powerful head of Mr. Zelensky’s office.

According to a survey conducted this summer by the Center for Social and Marketing Research in Kyiv, a majority of Ukrainians see corruption as having a stronger impact on the country than Russian bombings.

“These corruption scandals are terrible, and they are certainly demoralizing,” said Dmytro Kalach, 38, who works in light manufacturing and regularly donates money to the army.

He said that the graft would not deter him from continuing to support the military.

“The fact that they are scoundrels,” he said of government officials accused of corruption, “doesn’t mean I have to be a scoundrel like them.”

Some Ukrainians said they would carry on doing whatever it took to survive despite the corruption but still felt deeply hurt when cases came to light.

“I cannot simply shrug off these corruption scandals,” said Viacheslav Oksiuta, 68, a retiree from the military. He continues to work in the defense sector and is the father of two sons, one of whom is serving in the army.

“I can’t even watch television when I hear about these cases,” he said. “I take all of this very personally.”

Even as Parliament was taking action against Mr. Kravchenko this week, the drumbeat of corruption accusations carried on. Investigators said on Tuesday that they had discovered another illegal enrichment scheme, this time in a tax service office in western Ukraine.

item.title: Belarus Releases 25 Political Prisoners in Exchange for U.S. Easing of Sanctions
item.description:
Belarus on Wednesday released 25 political prisoners after a visit from President Trump’s envoy, continuing a thaw in relations between the United States and the eastern European nation’s autocratic leader, Aleksandr G. Lukashenko.

The prisoner release was the latest in a long series that began last year when the Trump administration, unlike the European Union, shifted away from sanctions against Belarus to embrace negotiations with Russia’s neighbor and closest ally.

The United States had hoped to get 200 people released on Wednesday. Despite getting far fewer freed, the Trump administration appeared to remain eager to push on with rapprochement, hoping that Mr. Lukashenko, a tough and cunning negotiator seasoned by years of dealing with the Kremlin, will release more later.

Wednesday’s prisoner release followed talks in Minsk between Mr. Lukashenko and the U.S. special envoy for Belarus, John Coale, a lawyer and friend of Mr. Trump with little previous government experience.

“Thank you, President Lukashenko, for this step,” Mr. Coale said on social media, adding that “we will continue to improve US-Belarus relations.”

Brussels and Washington, which used to denounce Mr. Lukashenko as “Europe’s last dictator,” started imposing sanctions on Belarus decades ago over human rights violations and other issues. They sharply expanded these after Belarus let Russia use its territory as a staging ground for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

While previous U.S. administrations believed that punishing Belarus would help push Mr. Lukashenko away from the Kremlin, that never happened. The Trump administration, which also wants Minsk to be less beholden to Moscow, sees Belarus as proof that its more transactional approach works, even if it has done little to loosen Mr. Lukashenko’s iron grip on the country.

This prisoners-for-sanctions relief deal was at least the fifth and followed the release of 250 prisoners in March in tandem with the removal of American sanctions on Belarus’ producers of potash fertilizer, the country’s largest source of export earnings.

Belarus’s state news agency, Belta, reported that, in exchange for the prisoners, Washington will lift sanctions on a state chemical company, Lakokraska, and a trading firm, Bellesbumprom.

Mr. Lukashenko, who has ruled Belarus since 1994, controls an expansive security apparatus that has arrested thousands of people since it began a brutal crackdown on dissent after nationwide street protests in 2020.

The protests followed implausible claims by Mr. Lukashenko to have won a landslide election victory, his sixth in a row, amid widespread reports of fraud. Last year, facing only phony regime-vetted candidates, he won yet another election, with more than 86 percent of the vote, an even bigger landslide.

Before Wednesday’s releases, the human rights group Viasna estimated that Belarusian jails held 916 political prisoners, down from 1,226 in February last year at the start of the U.S. rapprochement with Belarus.

In his talks with Mr. Coale, also attended by Ivan Tertel, the head of Belarus’ KGB security service, Mr. Lukashenko said his jails have no political prisoners, only criminals who broke the law, and urged the U.S. envoy not to believe “defectors spreading stories,” according to Belta.

Mr. Coale, the news agency reported, told Mr. Lukashenko that Mr. Trump “supports everything we do in every way.”

Those released on Wednesday, including three rock musicians, journalists and advocates of a Belarusian cultural identity separate from Russia, left Belarus for neighboring Lithuania.

From Belarus’s capital, Minsk, Mr. Coale traveled by car to Lithuania for talks with Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius that were expected to focus on the European Union’s continuing sanctions against Belarusian potash.

Belarus, which is landlocked, used to export much of its potash through the Lithuanian port of Klaipeda. The E.U. closed that route after the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine to punish Mr. Lukashenko for his support of Moscow and to force him to reconsider his close ties to the Kremlin.

Instead, the sanctions pushed him further into Russia’s orbit, as Belarus rerouted its exports through Russian ports.

Washington is hoping that the European Union will allow Belarus to resume potash shipments from Lithuania, which would help reduce global prices.

Releasing prisoners has not only helped Mr. Lukashenko dampen criticism against him in Washington, but it has also served his domestic political interests by undermining an exiled opposition movement led by Svetlana Tikhanovskaya, a former presidential candidate. She declared victory in the 2020 vote and then fled to Lithuania at the start of the post-election crackdown. She has since relocated to Warsaw.

Ms. Tikhanovskaya’s husband, Sergei, who was arrested before the vote to prevent him from running, was set free last year and has spent recent months feuding with his now estranged wife and her aides over their use of grant money provided by foreign governments.

He has complained bitterly that opposition media outlets controlled by Ms. Tikhanovskaya’s office have denigrated former prisoners like himself and Maria Kolesnikova, a popular opposition figure who was released from prison in December. She is viewed by many Belarusians as a symbol of courage and resistance because of her refusal to leave Belarus when authorities tried to forcibly expel her in 2020.

item.title: At Least 70 Die After Unofficial Gold Mine Collapses in Sudan
item.description:
Scores of people died and dozens of others were missing after shafts collapsed at an artisanal gold mine in Sudan, a charity group said on Wednesday.

It was the latest disaster connected to the lucrative but often lightly regulated business of low-tech mineral extraction in the region.

The mine in West Kordofan state collapsed on Sunday. Since then, 70 bodies have been recovered, but dozens of others remained trapped underground, said Suliman Abo Humeida, spokesman for the Emergency Response Rooms, a community-led humanitarian initiative, in the town of Al-Nuhud in West Kordofan.

“The chances of rescue are limited because there are no specialized rescue teams or specialized equipment,” Mr. Humeida said by telephone. He added that three people had been rescued, each with multiple fractures, and that most of the dead and missing were young men, though several were teenagers.

Artisanal gold mining is big business in Sudan and other countries in eastern Africa, including Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Workers use hand-held tools to dig vertical shafts 50 or more yards deep before building lateral tunnels from which earth is scooped and brought to the surface. Air is pumped down the shafts, in part to displace toxic gases, and the tunnels are braced with milled branches or lengths of wood to prevent collapse.

A series of interconnected shafts dug close to one another collapsed at the site in Al-Nuhud, according to Mr. Humeida.

The work is inherently dangerous, but with few other industries in the region, mining has become a major source of employment in the region. This is particularly true in Sudan, where a civil war that began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and a paramilitary group known as the Rapid Support Forces has shattered the country’s economy.

Gold is also a driver of the conflict between the Sudanese military and the Rapid Support Forces.

While individual miners earn little, they help to generate huge trade, fueled by high global gold prices. Since the war began, billions of dollars’ worth of gold has been shipped by both sides in the war to many countries.

Some of the profits are used to buy the missiles, guns and, increasingly drones, that have become central to the war.

The Rapid Support Forces have run one of the country’s most lucrative gold mines for almost a decade and control the area where the collapse took occurred on Sunday.
