item.title: E.U.-Canada Ambitions Face Reality Check
item.description:
The European Union’s invitation Wednesday for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc shows just how intent these traditional United States allies are on pursuing a more stable future by binding closer together.

“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said in the European Parliament in Strasbourg, a beaming Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada sitting just to her side. But there are no guarantees they will get there.

While details of what this relationship might look like remain scant, Ms. von der Leyen noted some potential areas of cooperation, including partnerships in manufacturing, technology, defense, energy policy and economic security.

This would not be “a partnership against anyone else,” she insisted, “but for our common strength.”

European officials said that, in the lead-up to the speech on Wednesday, the bloc wanted to ensure that President Trump did not see this new partnership with Canada as an anti-American move.

Still, if it isn’t precisely against the United States, then it’s unmistakably about it.

“Behind this is a desire to hedge against what for both partners is an increasingly fraught relationship with the United States,” said Ian Lesser, a distinguished fellow of the German Marshall Fund, based in Brussels.

“But it’s not just that it’s fraught,” he added. “It’s the most important geoeconomic and geopolitical relationship for both Europe and for Canada.”

For Mr. Carney, the invitation is both timely and symbolically important. He has decided to stand up to Mr. Trump, who has imposed tariffs on Canada and regularly threatens its sovereignty.

Mr. Carney has been pushing for Canada to get greater access to the European Union — its territory, its market, its funds and programs — without becoming a full member of the bloc.

He has found an enthusiastic partner in Ms. von der Leyen, who has painted Canada as a dependable source for Europe’s needs for energy and critical raw materials, as well as a steadfast ally who shares NATO membership, support for Ukraine and a commitment to the rule of law. Ms. von der Leyen does not represent the European Union’s 27 countries, but she sets the agenda for the bloc and commands its mighty bureaucracy.

The tie-up seems to make sense at a moment of global turbulence and a shifting global role for the United States. Between them, the European Union’s 27 members and Canada have more than 490 million citizens and include four of the world’s 10 largest economies.

The European Union is underpinned by dense, deep legal and procedural rules, built over decades by a group of nations that ceded sovereignty to one another, and to an unelected executive branch in Brussels.

Inserting a country an ocean away deeper into this web is not a straightforward business.

The label the European Union wants to confer on Canada, “associate member,” is not an existing type of partnership — meaning that it is not clear what actions Canada would have to take to earn it, or for it to be given.

“It has no legal basis,” said Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group. “It’s more symbolism and signal,” he added.

Ms. von der Leyen was taking a risk using the term, which had been floating for weeks ahead of her speech, and drew consternation from several member states, according to European officials.

It is seen as vague, untethered from legal frameworks and potentially antagonistic toward countries that already have detailed legal agreements with the European Union. These range from candidate nations such as Albania to close partners including Britain, Switzerland and Norway. Those countries have deep trade ties to the bloc and, in the case of Switzerland and Norway, have free movement into and out of other European nations.

Some Canadian officials do not appear to love the term, either, as membership in the European Union implies forfeiting some sovereignty, which is the opposite of what Mr. Carney has pledged to do. The Conservative opposition leader seized on the term, arguing that if Canada was never to be the 51st state of the United States, it should also not become the 28th member state of the European Union.

“There’s a lot of good will, but once one starts to look just a little bit closer, one also finds that many Europeans really don’t know Canada all that well, and they maybe aren’t fully taking on board Canada’s own sensitivities to sovereignty,” said Mr. Lesser.

Hours after Ms. von der Leyen spoke on Wednesday, the incoming Canadian ambassador to the European Union said that labels did not matter — but suggested that Canada preferred “alliance for the future” to describe the emerging new bond with the European Union. That phrase also appeared in Ms. von der Leyen’s speech.

“I think we’re still a ways away from actually landing on what we think the best way to describe it is,” said Jonathan Wilkinson.

Three European diplomats said that the title “associate member” may not stick.

Officials from both sides are working to find tangible progress that they hope to announce at a European Union-Canada summit scheduled to take place in Montreal at the end of October.

Two officials, one from the European Union and one from Canada, with knowledge of the talks, said that officials were trying hard to reach that goal, but that work had been slow and difficult, in part because it is highly technical.

Just how hard it can be to get the European Union to agree on anything has been displayed frequently over the years. For example, talks over a trade agreement with Mercosur, the South American bloc, lasted a quarter century.

Canada has its own experience with these E.U. rigidities — and has some of its own. Its free-trade agreement with the bloc, in effect in practice for a decade, has still not been ratified by 10 of the 27 member states, for various reasons.

Canada already participates in a handful of E.U. ventures, including Horizon, a technology and innovation research effort, and SAFE, a defense industrial program. It had to pay $100 million to participate in Horizon, and participation in other E.U. programs is also likely to require Canada to pay into a budget.

One more immediate benefit for Canada from closer ties to Europe may be in securing funding from the European Investment Bank. The major development bank, which is owned by the E.U. member states and has more than $630 billion in assets, is eager and ready to invest in Canadian projects, particularly in critical raw materials, and its leader is heading to Ottawa on Sunday to advance talks with the Canadian government.

The bank is ready to start work in Canada, a European official with knowledge of the preparations said, but needed Ottawa to approve certain administrative formalities such as allowing E.U. diplomats to work there.

Some of the ideas being discussed ahead of the October summit show the ambitious scope of the Canada-E.U. future relationship.

For example, officials said, Mr. Carney wants the bloc to work with Canada to build systems for payments and cloud computing that will offer an alternative to those of the United States in a bid to secure sovereignty.

Discussions have also been underway on a digital trade agreement, which could deepen cooperation on cybersecurity and regulatory cooperation.

Talks are more advanced to bring Canadian regulations in line with European ones in energy, including the monitoring, reporting and evaluation system used by the bloc to track methane emissions from vessels fueled by liquefied natural gas, as well as gas imports entering the European Union market. This is a necessity if Canada is going to export gas to the European Union.

Another area where Canada is particularly eager to see movement is the ability of its citizens to spend longer stretches of time in the European Union visa-free, have their professional qualifications recognized there and be able to study in European universities.

Because these policy areas hinge on complex and politically fraught immigration rules, major breakthroughs could be difficult. Additionally, any agreement improving Canadians’ access to Europe would require reciprocity, meaning that it would grant the same access to Canada for 450 million Europeans.

Some European diplomats have suggested that Erasmus — Europe’s popular student exchange program — could be an easier starting place for collaboration.

item.title: At Least 16 Dead in Gaza After Building Collapse, Officials Say
item.description:
A war-damaged building in Gaza collapsed on Wednesday, killing at least 16 people and trapping many more beneath the wreckage, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense rescue service.

Dozens were living in the complex, the Saada residential building in Gaza City, when it caved in at around 2 a.m. local time, officials from the service said. Civil Defense is a part of the Hamas-run interior ministry in Gaza.

The officials added that the building had previously been hit by an Israeli strike, though it was unclear when. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Search-and-rescue teams pulled survivors from the wreckage on Wednesday morning as they searched for missing residents.

“We can see people still trapped under the rubble,” said Raed al-Dahshan, director of Civil Defense in the Gaza City area, who is involved in the rescue efforts. “We’re doing everything we can to extract them.”

He said that the authorities in Gaza had warned residents that the building was unstable, but that many did not leave because they did not want to be displaced and potentially end up in worse conditions. Mr. al-Dahshan said that there were roughly 70 buildings in the Gaza City area at risk of collapse.

The deadly collapse underscores the devastation across Gaza, where years of punishing conflict between Israel and Hamas have left entire neighborhoods in ruins. Much of Gaza’s population was displaced by the conflict, and many are now living in damaged buildings.

After a U.S.-brokered cease-fire was agreed in October 2025, Palestinians had hoped that Israel would allow a significant amount of heavy machinery and construction materials into Gaza to begin the long process of removing rubble and rebuilding. Thousands of bodies remain missing beneath the rubble across Gaza from years of war, according to local officials.

Efforts by President Trump’s Board of Peace and regional mediators to advance the cease-fire and pave the way for reconstruction have stalled. Israel has continued to strike the territory, despite international pressure to halt its attacks there.

On Tuesday, an Israeli strike killed a Civil Defense worker and a teenager, according to an official in the rescue service. The Israeli military said it had been targeting Hamas militants, and that the attack was under review.

The International Committee of the Red Cross and Egyptian-backed rescue teams assisted local emergency crews on Wednesday in their search for survivors of the building collapse.

In a statement, Ramiz Alakbarov, the United Nations humanitarian coordinator for the occupied Palestinian territory, urged international authorities to allow heavy equipment into Gaza to assist in search-and-rescue operations, along with vital humanitarian aid.

“Every possible effort must be made to save lives, protect people from further harm and provide families with safer places to live,” he said. “Every minute counts.”

item.title: The Hidden Human Cost of Kim Jong-un’s New Power
item.description:
His nation is now a de facto nuclear power. Its economy is growing at the fastest pace in years. He has been courted by the leaders of China, Russia and the United States.

Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator, has emerged as an unlikely winner of the post-pandemic era. And his newfound strength rests on the systematic exploitation of his own people, which is actively facilitated by Moscow and Beijing.

By supplying troops and ammunition for Russia’s war in Ukraine, Mr. Kim is estimated to be reaping billions of dollars. Russia is repaying Pyongyang in advanced military technology and critical commodities like flour, pork and oil — goods his regime can then resell at home for profit.

But the human cost is staggering, for North Koreans at home and abroad.

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded on faraway battlefields.

“I tremble as I await the daily reports, wondering how many soldiers were lost, whether they suffered reckless losses in the pursuit of bravery, whether they succumbed to fear or fell captive to the enemy,” one young North Korean platoon leader wrote in his diary before he, too, died in combat.

Thousands more North Koreans toil behind the front lines, working in military drone factories, repairing war-damaged cities and building apartments across Russia to meet revenue quotas set by Mr. Kim’s government. With Moscow looking the other way to evade sanctions, many enter Russia on student visas but never see a classroom — instead sleeping in shipping containers and enduring 14-hour shifts with hardly any days off.

Closer to home, China is openly importing North Korean coal in violation of United Nations sanctions, satellite imagery indicates. Defectors say the commodity is mined by workers trapped in forced labor in central and northern North Korea.

Even North Korea’s biggest official export — hair products like wigs and false eyelashes, which are not subject to U.N. penalties — has brutal origins. Much of that merchandise is produced in labor camps, where inmates are forced to meet daily quotas and, survivors say, risk starvation if they fail. The payoff for Pyongyang was $188 million in sales to China in 2024 alone, according to Chinese customs data.

On paper, North Korea is a socialist state, with free provisions for citizens. In reality, it is a regime of quotas, in which everyone must contribute to a shadow economy that sustains Mr. Kim’s extravagant lifestyle and military ambitions — lavish dinners, armored cars, luxury yachts, seaside resorts and nuclear missiles.

“North Korea claims to be a tax-free country where everything is free,” said Ryu Hyeon-woo, who was its acting ambassador to Kuwait when he defected. “In reality, its system survives by milking its people.”

North Korea’s economy has grown more than 3 percent in each of the past three years, according to South Korea’s central bank, a drastic reversal from its pandemic-era contraction. To uncover the methods driving this turnaround, The New York Times spoke with dozens of North Korean defectors, human rights investigators and geopolitical analysts.

The first thing that Baek Hye-ok said she noticed at the Chongori labor camp in northeast North Korea was the smell.

A cell no larger than a two-car garage held more than 100 women. Wardens, unable to bear the stench of unwashed bodies, ordered inmates to kneel 10 feet away when summoned. Bedbugs dropped into bowls of gruel.

“You didn’t spit it out because your life depended on it,” Ms. Baek recalled years later in Seoul. “You never forget the stomach-churning smell when a bedbug bursts between your teeth.”

Work began at dawn. Young women with sharp eyesight stitched wigs and false eyelashes. Trucks delivered raw materials labeled in Chinese and departed with finished goods. Prison officials told inmates that the shipments went to China through the nearby city of Rason, Ms. Baek said.

“Your life depended on meeting your quota,” she said. “Fail, and you were beaten and your ration cut.”

During separate interviews, Ms. Baek and Lee Young-ju, another former inmate who defected and now lives in Seoul, said that roughly one in every 10 inmates died each year. They were quickly replaced by new arrivals — many of whom had been caught foraging for food across the border in China because they did not have enough to eat at home. Others were being punished for watching smuggled South Korean dramas. Some inmates were so desperate that they ate maggots from corpses. Ms. Lee spent three years at the labor camp while Ms. Baek put in two years over two stints.

“The place was a living hell,” Ms. Lee said.

Few can escape quotas, defectors say.

Villagers scour hills for berries bound for China. Schoolchildren supply rabbit hides for soldiers’ gloves. Tractor plants run dual lines: farm machinery on one, tanks on the other. Elites fund gold-plated statues of Mr. Kim’s father and grandfather, and maintain the Pyongyang mausoleum where their embalmed bodies lie. The 1.3-million-strong army — the world’s fourth largest — doubles as a free work force, dispatched to construction sites.

The scramble for revenue extends abroad.

Diplomats smuggle Cuban cigars and African rhino horns inside diplomatic pouches to raise “loyalty funds” for Mr. Kim, or to feed his family’s taste for Russian king crab, Arabian sweets and gold-tipped Montblanc pens, said Mr. Ryu, a son-in-law of the former head of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Bureau 39, which manages Mr. Kim’s secret funds.

Even the General Bureau of Reconnaissance — North Korea’s main intelligence agency — moonlights as a business. At one point, it ran restaurants and a squad of 19 hackers and IT workers out of the United Arab Emirates, Mr. Ryu said. They stole cryptocurrency or used stolen identities to take freelance coding jobs.

Pyongyang selects young students gifted in math and science, training them from an early age to become software engineers or hackers. It later deploys them to China, Russia and the Middle East, where they help fill the regime’s coffers while living in dormitories and being monitored by secret police. In the first four months of this year alone, they accounted for 76 percent of all cryptocurrency stolen worldwide, according to TRM Labs, an analytics company.

Mr. Ryu said a North Korean banking operative named Sim Hyon Sop had been central to laundering the earnings of these workers in the Middle East. The U.A.E.-based money-laundering network run by Mr. Sim and his Chinese partners has also been cited in U.S. court documents and a Treasury Department sanctions report.

Son Myong-hwa’s father labored underground in iron ore mines until lung disease claimed his life at 59. He spent days on end in the suffocating darkness of the pit, especially when the authorities raised production quotas. When Ms. Son arrived with lunchboxes, he and his co-workers were so caked in dust that “only their eyes and teeth flashed white when they smiled,” she said.

Mines serve as a dumping ground for those deemed lowest-class, including South Korean prisoners of war from the 1950s and their descendants — among them Ms. Son’s father and siblings.

Jeong Sun-nam, whose father and siblings worked mostly in iron ore mines, said her father survived three underground explosion accidents. When blasts shattered the shafts, she recalled, the miners’ wives clawed at the rubble with bare hands until their fingers bled.

“Minerals from North Korea are stained with blood,” said Ms. Jeong, who, like Ms. Son, managed to defect to South Korea.

Coal and iron-ore exports have long been an economic lifeline, though U.N. sanctions began squeezing the trade about a decade ago. Yet, smuggling has thrived, with ships cutting their tracking transponders and swapping illicit cargo in the open ocean. Satellite imagery analyzed last year by the London-based Open Source Center identified six repeat offenders ferrying North Korean coal and iron ore to Chinese ports.

Now even the pretense of secrecy is vanishing, especially after Russia and China dismantled in 2024 the U.N. panel monitoring sanctions enforcement.

A July report by the Citizens’ Alliance for North Korean Human Rights, a nonprofit based in Seoul, found that visits by large cargo ships to Nampo, North Korea’s primary coal and oil terminal, had surged fivefold since 2019. Blacklisted vessels no longer hide in the shadows — instead, the report said, they dock “openly” at Chinese terminals.

Lee Eun-pyong was a sergeant in North Korea’s 131st Guidance Bureau — the agency responsible for construction, security and uranium mining for North Korea’s nuclear program. In 2017 he was ordered to go to Russia and earn money for the regime. He said he and 33 of his comrades were heralded as “forefront warriors of the country’s nuclear power buildup.”

Their days in Moscow began at 7 a.m. and stretched past midnight, he said. The men slept on the dusty floors of unfinished buildings or crammed into shipping containers, chasing a mandatory monthly income quota of $600. On paper, he was enrolled at the European Institute Justo, a university in Moscow, but he was put to work laying bricks, making concrete slabs and plastering walls.

“We didn’t even know where the school was,” he recalled, after defecting to South Korea.

Under Mr. Kim, exporting laborers has become nearly every state agency’s side hustle. An estimated 100,000 North Korean workers remain in China, defying a 2019 U.N. repatriation deadline. Russia issued more than 36,000 entry visas to North Koreans last year — a fourfold jump from 2024 — nearly all for education, according to Russian government data. The Citizens’ Alliance and the Database Center for North Korean Human Rights, another nonprofit in Seoul, say that Pyongyang conspired with Russian schools like Sodeistvie College in Moscow to disguise workers’ labor in construction sites and sewing and meat-processing factories as “internships” and their wages as “scholarships.”

Today, Russian staffing agencies openly advertise North Korean workers for long shifts at textile mills, restaurants and farms. Job postings actively seek Korean interpreters. One Russian mayor said that demand for North Korean laborers — who “work like robots”— was so high that his city couldn’t afford them as street sweepers.

“We guarantee discipline: Employees work strictly according to the schedule, without smoke breaks or absences,” one staffing agency’s pitch reads. Another Moscow-area listing offered 40 North Korean women for hire, insisting that any future employer house them together — a condition their North Korean supervisors demand to prevent defections.

An investigation by the Dutch nonprofit Global Rights Compliance found that North Korean workers in Russia average 14-hour days, with some receiving only two days off a year. They live under the suffocating watch of security officers sent from Pyongyang. Three former workers, interviewed separately by The Times, recalled that the deepest sting was watching co-workers from Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia call their families freely while they could not.

To survive, the North Koreans dug through dumpsters for discarded clothes, they said. When one worker was sent home, others pressed letters into his hands for their families, with whatever money they had saved — usually a $20 bill — tucked inside. (The U.S. dollar is the most coveted currency in North Korea.)

During the pandemic, Pyongyang raised quotas and ordered laborers in Russia to keep working, citing the state’s own economic strain, according to a North Korean worker who fled Russia for South Korea in 2022. One man, he said, was escorted outside his work sites exactly once in five years — to buy gifts for his family the day before he finally went home.

“We were nothing but draft animals,” said the worker, who asked to be identified only by his last name, Han.

Last year, Ukrainian troops found a dead North Korean officer in Russia’s Kursk region. Documents recovered from his body exposed the predicament facing the estimated 16,000 North Korean troops Mr. Kim has dispatched to Russia — they were, essentially, cannon fodder. South Korean intelligence estimates that as many as 2,000 have been killed.

The documents — obtained by the Human Rights Foundation, a New York-based nonprofit — listed deployment plans, instructions and battlefield experiences of North Korean troops. A two-page document noted that some North Korean troops faced “a barrage of enemy artillery fire and suicide drones swarming in like a cloud of hornets.” When soldiers fell, their comrades often rushed to rescue them, disregarding enemy fire and suffering further casualties. Russian evacuation vehicles routinely took more than 10 hours to reach the wounded.

“Because of the failure to evacuate the wounded in time,” one document stated, “combatants were sacrificed during the evacuation.”

The account stands in stark contrast to the official narrative in North Korea, which glorifies the fallen as martyrs and claims that many had chosen to detonate hand grenades rather than risk capture while wounded.

The diary of the fallen platoon leader revealed the human cost of that pressure. Ukrainian special forces recovered the diary from the dead soldier and shared it with the Human Rights Foundation, where it was reviewed by a staff member who was a North Korean defector. In its pages, the officer alluded to his struggle between the duty to demonstrate “unparalleled bravery in battles” for “the greatest joy and satisfaction to the homeland and the party,” and a private fear that his ambition would ultimately cost his men their lives.

In December 2024, he wrote a final prayer for his fallen comrades. That same month, he wrote to his “princess” back home, leaving behind a promise in case he did not return.

If he died, he wrote, “I will become a butterfly and find you.”
